chapters.title: The First Voyage in Time
paragraphs: In 1895 a young English writer named Herbert George Wells published his first novel, and with it he invented one of the most powerful ideas in all of modern storytelling: the time machine. Before The Time Machine, no one had ever written about a vehicle built to carry a traveller deliberately backward and forward through time. Every time machine that has appeared since — in novels, in films, in comics — is a descendant of the strange brass-and-quartz contrivance that Wells set down in a laboratory in Richmond, in the last decade of the nineteenth century.

Wells was twenty-nine years old, a former science student who had studied biology under the great T. H. Huxley, “Darwin’s bulldog,” and who had worked as a teacher before turning to journalism. He took the newest and strangest idea of the physics of his day — that time might be a fourth dimension, differing in kind not at all from length, breadth, and thickness — and he asked the storyteller’s question: what if a man could travel in it the way he travels in space? The answer became this book: part scientific romance, part adventure story, and part dark prophecy about where the divisions of Wells’s own age might lead if they were carried to their logical end.

What follows is an essential selection of the novel — its most important scenes, told faithfully and in Wells’s own spirit, with his most famous passages given in his own words. It begins, as the novel begins, at a dinner table in London, where an inventor known only as the Time Traveller explains to his sceptical friends that he has built a machine for travelling through time — and then vanishes, to return from the year 802,701 with a tale of the beautiful, helpless Eloi, and of the blind, ape-like Morlocks who prey upon them in the dark.

chapters.title: The Time Traveller Explains
paragraphs: “The Time Traveller (for so it will be convenient to speak of him) was expounding a recondite matter to us.” So the novel opens, with no name for its hero — only his function. It is Thursday evening, and the narrator is dining at the Time Traveller’s house in Richmond, along with a small circle of familiar guests: the Medical Man, the Psychologist, the Provincial Mayor, the Very Young Man, Filby — red-haired and fond of argument — and the Editor of a well-known daily paper. The talk, as talk among clever Victorians will, has turned to the nature of time.

What makes the scene so daring, for 1895, is that the Time Traveller is not inventing his physics out of nothing. All through the 1880s and 1890s, mathematicians on both sides of the Atlantic had been playing seriously with the idea of a fourth dimension — publishing papers, giving lectures, arguing over geometries no human eye could ever see. Wells, fresh from his science studies, knew this talk well, and he puts it into his hero's mouth with the confidence of a man reporting news, not spinning fantasy. The fourth dimension was real mathematics; the machine was the fiction. That blend — hard science at the root, wild imagination flowering from it — is the formula Wells would use again and again, and it starts here, over the cigars, on a Thursday night in Richmond.

The narrator gives us the man as well as the theory: a brilliant, restless inventor, fond of paradox, the kind of friend whose after-dinner talk the others have learned to enjoy without quite believing. The Medical Man smiles into his cigar; the Psychologist leans forward, professionally interested; Filby sharpens his wits for the argument he loves. They have heard the Time Traveller's paradoxes before, and they are prepared to be amused. None of them — not even the narrator, who loves him best — is prepared to be convinced.

The Time Traveller’s claim is simple, and outrageous: “There is no difference between Time and any of the three dimensions of Space except that our consciousness moves along it.” A line drawn upon paper has length and breadth but no thickness; add thickness and you have a solid, which endures — which means, he argues, that it extends in a fourth direction as well: duration. “Our mental existences, which are immaterial and have no dimensions, are passing along the Time-Dimension with a uniform velocity from the cradle to the grave.” We are, all of us, travellers in time already — only we travel in one direction, at one unvarying pace, and we cannot steer.

To make it vivid he draws three lines upon the blackboard and speaks of the skeleton cubes by which mathematicians try to picture a fourth dimension: “You know how on a flat surface, which has only two dimensions, we can represent a figure of a three-dimensional solid, and similarly they think that by models of three dimensions they could represent one of four — if they could master the perspective of the thing.” He cites Professor Simon Newcomb, who had lately been expounding four-dimensional geometry to the New York Mathematical Society. The thing can be imagined, he insists; and what can be imagined can, perhaps, be built.

He presses the point home with an image the company cannot shake off: our lives, he says, are like sections cut at right angles through a four-dimensional body — each of us a sort of elongated shape stretching from the cradle to the grave through time, of which our consciousness perceives only one thin slice at a time, the present moment. We call the slices past, present, and future, and imagine them profoundly different; but the difference, he insists, is in us, not in them. It is our minds that move, not time that flows.

Filby objects, as Filby must: “If Time is really only a fourth dimension of Space, why is it, and why has it always been, regarded as something different? And why cannot we move in Time as we move about in the other dimensions of Space?” The Time Traveller smiles. Are we so free in space, he asks? Right and left, backward and forward we go freely enough — but up and down? Gravitation limits us there; and yet balloons are already beginning to defy even that. “Scientific people,” he says, “know very well that Time is only a kind of Space.” The barrier is not in nature, he suggests, but in ourselves.

And then he springs the trap he has been preparing all evening. If time is only a fourth dimension, then a machine ought to be able to move in it — a carriage that goes not across the country but across the centuries. “You can show black is white by argument,” says one of the guests dryly, and the table laughs; but the Time Traveller is in earnest. He has been at work upon such a machine for two years, he tells them, and it is nearly complete. Next Thursday, he promises, they shall see the proof — with their own eyes.

The evening breaks up at last with the argument still unsettled — Filby is still objecting on the doorstep, the Medical Man is laughing, the Editor is making notes for a paragraph. But the Time Traveller's final words linger with the narrator all the way home: next Thursday, the proof. For a week the little company talks of nothing else at their clubs — half mockery, half a strange, reluctant hope that the impossible might, just this once, be true.

There is, too, a strange intensity in the Time Traveller when he speaks of the machine itself — a light in his eyes that the narrator finds almost unsettling. He is not like a man describing a theory but like a man confessing a deed already half-done. Twice he breaks off in the middle of an argument to stare at the fire, as if listening for something the others cannot hear. The company laughs it off — genius is always a little odd, they agree — but the narrator, watching his friend, feels the first small chill of the evening: the suspicion that the Time Traveller is not amusing them with a paradox at all, but telling them, plainly and literally, the truth.

chapters.title: The Little Machine
paragraphs: The next Thursday the guests find their host not in the dining room but in the laboratory — a long, draughty room littered with the glorious clutter of invention. Upon the bench stands the machine itself, full-sized: “Parts were of nickel, parts of ivory, parts had certainly been filed or sawn out of rock crystal. The thing was generally complete, but the twisted crystalline bars lay unfinished upon the bench beside some sheets of drawings.” There is a saddle for the traveller to sit astride, and upon the bars before him a set of levers — one to drive forward through time, one to reverse, one to stop.

The laboratory itself is worth picturing, for it is the classic inventor's den of Victorian romance: a long room smelling of oil and ozone, benches crowded with half-built contrivances, coils of wire, bottles of chemicals, and drawings pinned and curling on every wall. In the midst of it the great machine squats like some brooding metal insect — all nickel bars and ivory and glittering quartz — with its saddle worn, the narrator notices, as if it had already been ridden. The Time Traveller catches his glance and smiles, and says nothing. It is a smile the narrator will remember later, on a very different night.

But the proof, tonight, is to be given with a model — “a glittering metallic framework, scarcely larger than a small clock, and very delicately made. There was ivory in it, and some transparent crystalline substance.” The Time Traveller sets it upon the table, explains the levers, and presses one of them with his finger. There is a breath of wind; the little machine spins, grows faint — and is gone. Vanished utterly from the table, while the lamp-flame leans and shivers in the draught of its going.

The Psychologist says quietly that it has gone into the future, and for a moment no one speaks. Then the Medical Man cries fraud — a conjuring trick, the thing slipped away by sleight of hand. Filby argues the physics; the Editor asks practical questions about return tickets and whether one might profit from foreknowledge. The Time Traveller only smiles his tired smile. The large machine, he says, wants only the finishing of the quartz rods. When it is done, he means to go himself — to see with his own eyes what lies ahead of mankind in time.

The guests crowd round the empty table, half-laughing, half-uneasy. The Medical Man gets down on his knees to look for wires; the Psychologist taps the table-top and finds it solid; Filby declares it a trick and demands to see it done again, which the Time Traveller, smiling, declines to do — the model, he says, has gone where it has gone, and will not return for a very long time. The lamp still smokes where the little machine stood. Nobody, quite, likes to say what he is thinking.

A week passes. On the Thursday following, the narrator arrives for dinner to find the other guests already assembled — and the host missing. Half past seven comes, and with it no Time Traveller; the guests fall upon the dinner without him, grumbling good-naturedly. And then, at last, he stumbles in through the French window: his coat dusty and smeared with green, his hair disordered, his face haggard and streaked, one foot bare and bleeding, limping as if he had walked through ruin. He says nothing at first. He eats — ravenously, wolfishly, like a starving man — drinks a great draught, lights a cigar, and looks round the table. Then he announces that he has a story for them: the story of what the Time Machine has done.

He will not begin his story until he has eaten — a starved man, the narrator thinks, watching him — and drunk, and smoked half a cigar in silence, staring into the fire. The guests exchange glances: whatever has happened to their friend, it has marked him. There is a new look in his eyes, the narrator says — the look of a man who has seen something no other living man has seen. At last the Time Traveller sets down his cigar, and tells them, from the beginning, exactly what befell him.

The argument that follows the demonstration lasts half the night and settles nothing. Filby insists it was legerdemain — the little thing whisked away by a hidden thread, no doubt — while the Psychologist, pale and thoughtful, keeps returning to the draught of wind that had leaned the lamp-flame: a conjuror's thread, he says quietly, does not stir the air. The Medical Man, ever practical, wants to know only one thing: if the machine truly went forward in time, why did it not come back? To which the Time Traveller answers, with that odd light in his eyes again, that perhaps it has not finished going yet.

chapters.title: The Rush Through the Ages
paragraphs: He tells them how, that very morning, he mounted the machine in the laboratory, settled himself in the saddle, and took the starting lever in his hand. He had meant only a short trial — a little way into the future and back. “I pressed the lever over to its extreme position. The night came like the turning out of a lamp, and in another moment came to-morrow.”

The horror of it, he says, was not only the speed but the helplessness — the knowledge that he had loosed a power he could not call back. His stomach turned as on a ship in a storm; his head rang; and through it all ran the absurd, practical fear of a man who has done something irreversible: what if the levers jammed? What if he could never stop at all, but must hurtle onward forever, watching the sun flicker and the ages stream past, until he starved in the saddle or went mad? He laughs as he tells it — a short, uneasy laugh — but the guests do not laugh with him.

What followed, he says, he can hardly describe: “I am afraid I cannot convey the peculiar sensations of time travelling. They are excessively unpleasant. There is a feeling exactly like that one has upon a switchback — of a helpless headlong motion! I felt the same horrible anticipation, too, of an imminent smash.” He clung to the machine as the world dissolved around him, afraid to look, afraid to let go, while the lever seemed to press itself ever harder forward.

When at last he dared to look, day and night were chasing each other across the laboratory windows faster than the eye could follow — “the sun hopped swiftly across the sky, and every minute marking a day.” Presently, as his speed increased, the flickering merged into one: “the palpitation of night and day merged into one continuous greyness; the sky took on a wonderful deepness of blue, a splendid luminous colour like that of early twilight; the jerking sun became a streak of fire, a brilliant arch, in space; the moon a fainter fluctuating band.” The walls of the laboratory melted and vanished; he was in the open air. Trees grew and withered in instants; great buildings rose, aged, and fell like castles of cloud; snow flashed white across the land and was gone. On the dials before him the hands spun — years, decades, centuries devoured in moments.

And human history itself unrolled beneath him like a panorama run mad. He saw great buildings rise where the laboratory had stood — saw them age, crumble, and give place to others stranger still; saw the valley clothed and unclothed with forests; saw winter snows flicker across the land like white heartbeats, each flash a year. Empires, he thought, must have risen and fallen in the instants between his blinks — whole civilisations blooming and rotting while he clung to his saddle, a spectator outside of time.

A wild fear seized him then — that if he stopped he might materialise inside some solid thing, embedded in rock or masonry. But the machine was rushing on, and he had to chance it. Gritting his teeth, he reversed the lever gently, braking his headlong flight through the ages. Hail began to sting his face; the spinning dials slowed; the roaring in his ears died away. He looked down at the date-dials, and his heart hammered: they stood at 802,701. He had travelled more than eight hundred thousand years into the future — and the machine stood at rest upon a rain-swept lawn, in a world he did not know.

By the end he was sick and giddy, his hands numb on the levers, his ears full of a roaring like a great wind. Every instinct screamed at him to stop — and every reason warned him that to stop blindly might be death, that he might find himself embedded in the heart of a rock, or dropped into mid-air above some vanished street. But he could bear the flight no longer. He chose his moment as a man chooses where to leap from a runaway horse — and pulled the lever home.

And then the stopping was itself a kind of violence. The hail that met him was real hail, stinging real flesh; the wind of that far-off winter cut through his clothes; and when the machine shuddered to rest, he sat for a full minute with his eyes shut, afraid to open them. When he did, the laboratory was gone — walls, benches, lamps, all gone — and in its place this strange, sweet, sunlit garden, with the rain-washed sphinx watching him. He had done it. Against all reason, against all the sober physics of his century, he had done it — and the first thing he felt, he confesses, was not triumph but a vast and desolate homesickness.

chapters.title: The Year 802,701
paragraphs: The hail passed, and he looked about him. He stood in a vast, neglected garden — flowers run wild, great trees, no paths kept — and beyond it, on a hill, rose colossal buildings of glittering, rain-washed stone, their windows dark, their lines strange and ruined. Between him and the river that wound through the valley stood a colossal figure in white stone, set upon a pedestal of bronze: a winged sphinx, blind-eyed, smiling its eternal enigmatic smile down at him across eight hundred millennia. The air was warm and sweet, though it was — by his reckoning — the depth of winter. There was no smoke, no road, no sign of work or traffic anywhere.

The sphinx holds him longest. It is not beautiful — its blind stone face is cruel, almost mocking — and yet he cannot look away from it. Later he will understand why it troubles him so: it is the one thing in all this soft, decaying world that seems to know something. Its great wings are folded; its lion's paws rest on the bronze pedestal; and beneath its enigmatic smile, behind the sealed bronze doors, wait the answers to every question he has not yet learned to ask. For now it is only a statue, huge and white against the green — but he will dream of it, in the nights to come, with its stone eyes open.

And then, coming toward him through the long grass, he saw the people of this future age. “He was a slight creature — perhaps four feet high — clad in a purple tunic, girdled at the waist with a leather belt. Sandals or buskins — I could not clearly distinguish which — were on his feet; his legs were bare to the knees, and his head was bare.” Beautiful they were, with a soft, hairless, childlike beauty — Dresden-china pretty, the Time Traveller thought — and dressed alike in soft robes, without distinction of sex that he could see. They laughed at him, a rippling musical laughter, crowded round to touch his clothes and his hands, and spoke to him in a soft, cooing tongue of which he understood not a word.

He tries to talk to them — slow gestures, pointing, smiling — and they answer with peals of delighted laughter, as if he were a clever pet performing tricks. One of them, bolder than the rest, pats his face with a soft hand; another tries on his jacket and parades in it to general applause. Their speech is music without meaning to him — a rippling of vowels — though after a day or two he catches a word for themselves, soft as a sigh: Eloi. It is the only name they seem to need.

They were fruit-eaters, these little people — the Eloi, as he would learn to call them — and they led him, chattering, to one of the great ruined halls, where hundreds of them sat at long stone tables eating nothing but fruit: great white blossoms and sweet pulpy produce gathered from the wild gardens. There was no cooking, no kitchen, no labour of any kind that he could discover. No old people among them, no sick, no maimed — all young, all lovely, all idle. They wore flowers; they sang wordless little songs; they slept where they would.

His first theory formed itself quickly, and it pleased him. Mankind, he thought, had at last conquered nature — had banished disease, want, and danger — and had settled into a long, golden afternoon of ease. The struggle for existence was over; the too-perfect security of this world had let its people soften into mere beautiful futility. It was, he thought, the triumph he had always dreamed of: humanity come into its kingdom. Only one small thing troubled the picture, and at first he laughed at himself for noticing it — the way the little people glanced, again and again, toward the gathering dark, and the way their laughter died as the sun went down.

In the great hall that evening he sits among hundreds of them at the long stone tables, eating the strange fruit they press upon him, while the light fails softly through the broken roof. No one says grace; no one serves; no one, so far as he can see, is in charge of anything at all. It is all ease and plenty and gentle laughter — and yet, as the shadows lengthen across the tables, he notices again that small, repeated gesture: the quick glance toward the dark doorways, the laughter dying, the little hands reaching for one another in the gloom.

His first night in the future he spends in one of the great halls, among the sleeping Eloi, and it is stranger than anything he has yet seen. They have no beds, no privacy, no ceremony of retiring: as the light fails they simply lie down where they are, in heaps and clusters, like tired children, and sleep the instant, dreamless sleep of the utterly carefree. He lies awake long after the hall is dark, listening to their soft breathing, and thinking of London — of his house, his laboratory, his friends at dinner — eight hundred thousand years away, as distant now as a story heard in childhood. When sleep comes at last, he dreams of falling through endless blue twilight.

chapters.title: The Eloi and Their Fear
paragraphs: In the days that followed he lived among the Eloi and learned their simple tongue, little by little. They had no books, no writing, no tools, no memory of any past. Their clothes were of soft woven fibre, but no one wove; their fruit came from the gardens, but no one gardened. They slept together in the great halls, hundreds in a company, like children in a dormitory. And as the light failed each evening, a change came over them: the laughter stopped, they huddled close, and none — not one — would venture out into the darkness. A little one would weep at a shadow. Their fear of the dark was absolute, instinctive, and — so far as he could see — utterly without cause.

He explores the great halls by daylight, trying to understand how this world feeds and clothes itself, and finds — nothing. No kitchens, no workshops, no granaries, no tools of any kind. The stone tables are ancient beyond reckoning; the robes the Eloi wear are soft but fraying, as if woven in some unimaginably distant past and never replaced. It is as though the whole race were living, heedless and happy, on the interest of some vast capital laid up by their ancestors — eating the fruit of gardens planted by hands long dust, wearing the clothes of the dead. And the capital, he begins to fear, is running out.

Their days are one long, purposeless playtime. They have simple games — dancing in circles, tossing flowers, wading in the shallows — and a kind of wordless singing, sweet and melancholy, that drifts across the gardens at noon. But nothing is made, nothing mended, nothing learned. He looks in vain for children and for old people: all are young, all are of an age, as if the race had settled into a single, unchanging generation and simply — stopped. It is beautiful, and it is profoundly unnatural, and the longer he watches, the less it pleases him.

For what was there to fear? The world seemed empty of all danger. No beast prowled the gardens; no enemy threatened the halls. And yet the fear was real, and it was old — older than memory, worn into the very marrow of these gentle people. Puzzling over it, the Time Traveller began to notice things he had missed: here and there upon the hillsides stood round towers like wells, rimmed with bronze, from which a curious throbbing draught of air rose ceaselessly, carrying with it a faint, rhythmic thumping, as of great engines working far below. Something lived underground. Something worked, down in the dark, while the Eloi played in the sun.

And then came the blow that changed everything. Returning one evening to the lawn where he had left his machine, he found the turf torn — and the machine gone. Dragged, by the marks in the grass, across the lawn to the bronze pedestal of the White Sphinx, whose panels — he now saw — were not solid bronze but doors, shut fast. Rage and panic seized him together: without the machine he was stranded eight hundred thousand years from home, a castaway in time. He beat upon the bronze doors until his hands bled; the Eloi watched him with mild, uncomprehending pity. At last he forced himself to think. The machine was inside the pedestal; the pedestal could be forced open — but not tonight, and not alone. First he must understand this world, and above all he must understand what came up out of those wells when the sun went down.

That night he lies awake in the great hall, listening. Above the soft breathing of the sleepers he can hear it, faint but unmistakable, carried up through the stone: the throb and thump of machinery, patient and endless, from somewhere far below. And once — he is sure of it — a sound like a soft footfall in the corridor outside, and a gleam of eyes that are not Eloi eyes, gone before his match flares. Weena, asleep against his arm, whimpers in her dreams and clutches him tighter.

Weena tries to warn him, in her small way, about the wells. She will not go near them even by day; when he walks toward one, she pulls at his sleeve with real terror, pouring out a stream of soft, urgent words he cannot follow. Once he laughs and lifts her up to peer over the rim — and she screams, a thin, terrible scream, and buries her face in his shoulder and will not be comforted for an hour. After that he does not laugh. He begins to keep a match ready in his pocket whenever the sun goes down — though he could not, just then, have said why.

chapters.title: Weena
paragraphs: It was by the river, a day or two later, that the little woman came into his life. She had been bathing in a shallow reach, and the current — stronger than it looked — had caught her and was sweeping her, shrieking thinly, toward the deeper water. She was drowning, plainly drowning, not twenty yards from a crowd of her own people — and not one of them moved. They stood on the bank and watched her with mild, vacant interest, as they might have watched a falling leaf. The Time Traveller tore off his jacket, plunged in, fought the current, and dragged her, gasping and half-conscious, ashore. The onlookers applauded prettily, as at a clever trick, and went back to their flowers.

She is full of small, solemn ceremonies that delight him. Every morning she examines his face with grave attention, as if to make sure he has not changed in the night; every evening she arranges her garlands with the care of a priestess. She has a clear, high laugh like a bell, and when he does something that pleases her — catches a flower she has thrown, or repeats one of her words correctly — she claps her hands with pure joy. In all his life, the Time Traveller says, looking round the dinner table with eyes suddenly bright, he has never been loved so simply and so completely as he was loved, for those few days, by Weena.

He carries her up the bank and lays her on the grass, and she clings to him, gasping, her little hands twisted in his wet sleeve — while her own people stand round in a ring and watch, smiling their empty smiles, as if a rescue were merely another entertainment. It strikes him then, with a sudden cold clarity, what he has already half-guessed: that kindness itself has withered in these people, along with courage and curiosity. They are gentle because nothing has ever required them to be anything else — not because they are good.

Her name, he learned, was Weena — the first Eloi whose name he knew — and from that hour she attached herself to him with the absolute devotion of a child or a dog. She followed him everywhere, trotting at his heels; she wove garlands of white flowers and hung them round his neck until he walked wreathed like a sacrifice; she slept at night with her head upon his arm, her little hand fast in his sleeve. She had, he thought, the sweetest nature he had ever known — all tenderness and trust, untouched by fear of him, this strange grey giant from the dawn of time.

But Weena, too, knew the terror of the dark. When evening fell she would cling to him and sob, pressing her face into his coat, whispering words he could not understand — pleas, warnings. Once, when he made as if to go out after sunset, she threw herself before him in an agony of distress. Whatever walked the night of this world, Weena knew it, and her whole small body remembered it. He held her close, and made her a promise in the silence of his heart: when he broke open the pedestal and took back his machine, he would not leave her behind in this beautiful, terrible place. He would carry her with him — back through eight hundred thousand years — to safety.

In the days that follow she becomes his shadow and his comfort. She learns a few of his words and lisps them proudly; she is terrified of his Time Machine and will not go near it; every morning she comes to him crowned with fresh flowers, grave as a little queen at a ceremony. He finds himself talking to her as one talks to a child — telling her of London, of the sea, of winter snow — though she understands almost nothing. And he watches her with a growing ache, for he alone, of all the smiling Eloi, seems to know what the darkness holds for them.

But there are moments when the shadow falls across even her sunshine. Sometimes, in the middle of her play, she will stop and listen — head tilted, like a small animal — to some sound too faint for his ears, and the light will go out of her face. Sometimes at night she wakes screaming from dreams she cannot tell him, and he must hold her and rock her like a child until the trembling stops. He asks her, in his halting Eloi, what frightens her; and she answers with one word, whispered, that he comes to dread as much as she does — the word for the dark, and for what walks in it.

chapters.title: The Palace of Green Porcelain
paragraphs: Far across the valley, glinting green in the sunlight, stood a building unlike the others — vast, low, shimmering with a strange iridescence. The Eloi had a soft name for it which he rendered in his own mind as the Palace of Green Porcelain, and thither he resolved to go, with Weena trotting faithfully at his side. For he was now certain of one thing: the little people knew nothing and remembered nothing, but the stones of their world might remember for them. If any record of what mankind had been — and of what had happened to it — survived anywhere, it would be there.

The fossil hall stops him longest. The monsters tower over him — skeletons of creatures no human eye ever saw alive, their bones yellow with age, their jaws still grinning after a hundred million years. He thinks of the men who dug them up and set them here, proud of their science, sure that knowledge would last forever — and he thinks of the dust in the library, and of Weena putting flowers in his pockets, and he feels a pity so deep it is like grief. All their wisdom, all their wonder, and it ends in this: a picnic ground for butterflies who cannot read.

The palace was a museum — the museum of a dead civilisation. He walked through hall after hall of it in gathering awe and desolation: the colossal skeleton of some extinct monster towering overhead; galleries of rust-eaten machines, their purposes forgotten; glass cases of minerals and shells; and then, most poignant of all, the library — or what had been a library — where the books themselves had rotted to brown dust that crumbled at the touch of his finger. All the knowledge, all the poetry, all the science of mankind, turned to mould. He stood among the ruins of human thought, and Weena, uncomprehending, put flowers into his pockets to cheer him.

In the gallery of machines he wanders among the skeletons of a mechanical age: great engines eaten through with rust, instruments of forgotten purpose, a rusted cylinder that might have been a gun, or a pump, or a god. Here, he thinks, is the whole material triumph of mankind — the conquest of nature by machinery — ended as a museum exhibit for no one. The Morlocks below still tend some remnant of it, blindly, out of habit; but the age that built it is as dead as the monsters in the fossil hall.

But in a side gallery — a gallery of old chemistry and physics, of the practical arts — he found treasure. A box of matches: real matches, dry and usable after eight hundred thousand years, in a sealed case. And beside it a lump of camphor, which burns with a fierce white flame. Fire! The thought blazed up in him like the thing itself: with fire he could hold the darkness at bay; with fire he was no longer helpless. He pocketed the matches and the camphor with the care of a miser. And from among the rusting exhibits he chose himself a weapon — a stout bar of metal, heavy as a mace — and hefted it in his hand. But as the light faded in those vast dead halls, his triumph curdled into dread: twice he caught a glimpse of pale eyes watching from the shadows, and Weena was trembling, pulling at his sleeve, begging him without words to leave. They hurried out into the last of the daylight, and he resolved: at dawn he would force the bronze doors of the pedestal and take back his own.

As they leave, the light is going, and the palace seems to watch them go. Twice on the long walk back Weena stops dead, her hand tightening on his, staring at nothing he can see among the trees. Once he hears it too — a faint pattering, off to the left, keeping pace with them just beyond sight. He grips his iron bar and quickens his step, and does not let go of her hand until they are safe among the crowds in the lighted hall.

The finding of the matches is the novel's great turning point, and Wells gives it the weight of a miracle. The Time Traveller works the sealed case open with trembling fingers — half-convinced the sticks will crumble — and then, holding his breath, strikes one against the box. It flares! A tiny, everyday, nineteenth-century flame, burning steadily in the year 802,701 — and Weena cries out with delight and dances round it, and the Time Traveller, that hard-headed man of science, feels his eyes sting. It is the first familiar thing he has seen since he left home: fire, the oldest friend of man, come back to him across eight hundred thousand years.

chapters.title: The Morlocks
paragraphs: But first he had to know what lived below. Choosing one of the round well-towers, he gripped its rim, found the metal rungs set into its side, and lowered himself down into the throbbing dark. The shaft dropped a hundred feet or more; the air that beat upward past him was warm and foul, carrying a smell he did not like to name. At the bottom, a narrow passage opened into a vast, low cavern lit by a dim red glow — and there, among great thumping machines, he saw them at their work.

What appals him most in the cavern is not the Morlocks themselves but their industry — the dreadful, mindless diligence of it. The great machines thump and turn, tended by white hands that never rest; half-finished work lies about — cloth, it looks like, and metal parts — produced for no one he can see, wanted by no one, in a world where no one wants anything. It is labour continuing from sheer habit, eight hundred thousand years after its purpose died: the ghost of the factory system, still working its endless shift in the dark.

The rungs are worn smooth by — something — that climbs them often. Halfway down, the stench meets him fully: a thick, meaty smell, like a butcher's shop left too long in the sun, that turns his stomach. Below, the red glow resolves itself into furnace mouths along the cavern wall, and the thumping into the beat of vast machines, tended by flitting white shapes that work with a terrible, mindless industry. He strikes a match — and the whole cavern seems to flinch.

“It was a dull white, and had strange large greyish-red eyes; also there were fluff of hair on its head and back. But, as I say, it went too fast for me to see distinctly. I cannot tell if it ran on all-fours, or only with its forearms held very low.” So he describes the first Morlock he ever saw clearly — a blind, ape-like thing, human in its shape and horrible in its difference, that scuttled away from his match-flame with a chittering cry. There were more of them in the dark beyond counting: he could hear them, smell them, feel their eyes upon him. They shrank from his light — these were creatures of absolute darkness — but they were curious, and bold, and hungry-looking; one of them snatched at his box of matches, and he fled up the shaft with his heart hammering, hauling himself hand over hand into the blessed sunlight.

Now, at last, the pieces fell together, and the truth of this world stood clear before him — clear and hideous. Mankind had not remained one; it had split, as all things split under pressure, along the oldest fault-line of all: the division between those who labour and those who do not. “So, in the end, above ground you must have the Haves, pursuing pleasure and comfort and beauty, and below ground the Have-nots, the Workers getting continually adapted to the conditions of their labour.” The rich and idle had drifted, over hundreds of thousands of years, into the lovely, helpless Eloi; the workers, driven ever deeper underground to tend the machines, had become the blind, nocturnal Morlocks. Two species, from one stock — the aristocrat and the labourer, each degenerated to the logical end of his kind.

Climbing back into the daylight, shaken and filthy, he works out the history of it in his mind. It began, he thinks, in his own century: the growing gulf between rich and poor, the rich withdrawing ever further into pleasure and idleness, the poor driven ever deeper into the factories and mines — until the exchange between class and class, the mingling that had kept mankind one species, ceased altogether. Then time did the rest. Above ground, ease without effort; below ground, labour without light. Eight hundred thousand years of it — and here is the result, as neat as a sum in arithmetic.

His escape up the shaft is the narrowest thing in the book. The Morlocks recover from their fear of the match-flame sooner than he hoped — he hears them gathering below, chittering with excitement — and twice a cold hand closes on his ankle as he climbs. He kicks free, scrabbling upward with bleeding hands, expecting every moment to be dragged down into the red-lit dark; and when he rolls over the rim at last into the clean sunlight, he lies on the grass laughing and gasping like a madman, while the Eloi gather round to stare at this strange grey giant who climbs out of wells.

chapters.title: The Terrible Truth
paragraphs: “The great triumph of Humanity I had dreamed of took a different shape in my mind. It had been no such triumph of moral education and general co-operation as I had imagined. Instead, I saw a real aristocracy, armed with a perfected science and working to a logical conclusion the industrial system of to-day. Its triumph had not been simply a triumph over Nature but a triumph over Nature and the fellow-man.” So the Time Traveller writes in his journal, and the words are the hinge of the whole book. The golden age he had dreamed of was no golden age at all, but the end-product of his own century’s factory system, worked out remorselessly across geological time: above, the consumers, refined into useless beauty; below, the producers, degraded into subterranean apes.

He spells the theory out in his journal, step by step, as a man of science should: first, the slow separation of mankind into two castes — the idle rich above, the labouring poor below — already far advanced in his own Victorian England; then the ending of all mingling between them, as the rich grow ever richer in refinement and the poor ever poorer in everything but toil; then the long, slow divergence, generation upon generation, until the two castes can no longer even be called one species. It is evolution, he sees — blind, pitiless evolution — doing exactly what it always does with isolated populations: making them strange to each other. Only here the isolating barrier was not an ocean or a mountain range, but money.

He writes it all down that night in his journal, by the light of a single precious match, while the Eloi sleep around him: the two species, the wells, the machines, the white apes in the dark. Setting it out in order does not make it less horrible; if anything, the neatness of the explanation is the most horrible thing of all. There is no mystery left, no comforting doubt — only the logic of his own age, followed faithfully to its end.

And then, sitting alone in the dark of the great hall with Weena asleep against his shoulder, the last and worst piece of the puzzle clicked into place. The Morlocks clothed the Eloi — for where else did those soft robes come from? The Morlocks, somehow, fed the Eloi — for the fruit did not gather itself. Why would the blind workers of the underworld tend and clothe the useless idlers of the daylight, unless — “The flesh I had seen in the Under-world! It had seemed faintly human.” He had seen meat down there, in the Morlock caverns — meat, in a world without cattle. “Even at the time, I remember, I was convinced that my explanation was right.”

The Eloi were cattle. That was the whole of it, and it explained everything: the Morlocks’ care of them, the Eloi’s instinctive terror of the dark, the empty nights when some sleeper would simply not be there in the morning, and no one would ask where she had gone. On certain moonless nights the Morlocks came up out of the wells and took what they needed — as men take sheep from a fold. Weena’s sobs, her clinging hands, her agony when he turned toward the darkness: she knew. Her whole race knew, in their bones, what the dark was for. He held the sleeping child closer, and his pity turned to a cold and murderous resolve. Fire was his weapon, and he had fire. He would break the bronze doors, take back his machine — and take Weena out of this charnel-house world forever.

And Weena — what of Weena? The thought of her small, trusting face steadies him like a hand on his shoulder. He will not leave her to the wells and the moonless nights. His plan takes shape, cold and clear: at first light he will force the bronze doors with his iron bar, drag out the machine, and then — with fire in his pockets and Weena beside him — he will quit this world forever. It is a good plan. It does not occur to him, yet, that the Morlocks may have plans of their own.

And the final elegance of it — the thing that makes him put down his pen and stare into the dark — is how perfectly it explains Weena's people. Their beauty: the beauty of things bred for no purpose but to be looked at, like flowers. Their helplessness: the helplessness of creatures that have never needed to help themselves. Even their fear of the dark is explained — not a superstition but a racial memory, the inherited knowledge of prey. Every detail fits. That is what horrifies him most of all: not that the truth is strange, but that it is so completely, so terribly reasonable.

chapters.title: The Night of Fire
paragraphs: They set out for the White Sphinx at dawn, but the way was long, and night overtook them in the forest between the palace and the sphinx. He would not risk the open dark with Weena, so he made a camp: he gathered dry wood into a great pile, and with his precious matches and the fierce-burning camphor he kindled a fire — a roaring, crackling wall of flame against the night. Beyond its light he could hear them gathering: the soft patter of naked feet on the forest floor, the chittering whispers, the gleam of great grey-red eyes. The Morlocks feared the flame — they circled and shrank from it — but they were many, and they were patient, and they were hungry.

The burning of the forest is one of the great set-pieces of early science fiction, and Wells writes it with all his powers. The fire goes up like a living thing — a roaring wall, a hundred feet high, racing through the dry undergrowth faster than a man can run, with the Morlocks fleeing before it like white moths before a lamp, shrieking, blundering, beating at the flames with their bare hands. The heat is like the door of a furnace; the smoke turns the moon the colour of blood; and through it all the Time Traveller stands his ground in the clearing, a blackened figure with a blazing brand in each hand, guarding the one small life he has sworn to protect.

They come in rushes — a patter, a pause, a sudden scurry at the edge of the light — testing him. He meets each rush with a blazing brand thrust into the dark, and each time they fall back, shrieking, shielding their great pale eyes. Weena crouches behind him, her face buried in his coat, whimpering with every sound. Once a bolder one darts almost into the firelight, and he brings the iron mace down — and is sick at what he has done, even as he does it. They are horrible; but they were men, once.

Then came the disaster. Whether a spark was carried by the wind, or whether the Morlocks themselves — maddened by hunger — drove the fire outward, he never knew; but all at once the dry undergrowth caught, and in minutes the whole forest was ablaze. A wall of fire raced through the trees; the night became day, red and roaring; smoke rolled black across the stars. The Morlocks, blinded and terrified, blundered shrieking through the inferno, and he fought them off with blazing brands, swinging his iron mace, with Weena clinging to his coat. And then — in the smoke, in the rush, in one blind moment of turning — her hand slipped from his. He called her name into the roar; he beat back through the burning wood calling and calling; but there was no answer. Weena was gone — lost in the fire, or taken in the confusion — and he never saw her again.

Dawn came at last, grey through the smoke, upon a blackened and silent forest. Alone now, scorched and half-blinded, the Time Traveller walked the last miles to the White Sphinx. And there — miracle or trap — the bronze doors of the pedestal stood open. He did not hesitate: he stepped into the dark within, and the doors clashed shut behind him. They were waiting in the blackness — clutching hands, chittering mouths — but he had his mace, and he swung it in the dark with all the strength of grief and rage, and fought his way to where his machine stood. He flung himself into the saddle, tore at the lever — and as the Morlocks closed in, the world lurched, spun, and fell away beneath him. He was in time again, and free.

When the fire has burned itself out he searches the blackened wood for hours, calling until his voice breaks — turning over charred branches with trembling hands, dreading what he might find, dreading more the finding of nothing. Nothing: no trace of her at all. Whether the flames took her, or the Morlocks in the confusion, he never learns. He walks on toward the sphinx at last with empty hands and a hollow chest, and the two white flowers she put in his pocket that morning are the only part of her he will ever carry home.

The fight in the pedestal is fought in utter darkness, and it is the most desperate passage in the book. The bronze doors have closed behind him; the air is thick with the smell of the Morlocks; cold hands pluck at his clothes, his hair, his face. He cannot see — he can only swing, again and again, striking soft bodies that give way with sickening sounds, while the chittering rises to a scream. Then his groping hand finds the cold quartz of the machine — the saddle, the levers — and he throws himself across it, wrenching the starting lever over even as the hands close on his throat. The darkness spins. The hands fall away. He is rising — falling — through time itself, and the Morlocks are gone.

chapters.title: The End of All Things
paragraphs: But he did not stop. Mad with grief, sick with horror at what he had seen, he drove the machine onward — further, ever further into the future — as if he could outrun the memory of Weena and the Morlocks. Millions of years unrolled beneath him. At last, his strength failing, he braked the machine to a halt — and stepped out upon a lonely beach at the end of the world. “The sky was no longer blue. North-eastward it was inky black, and out of the blackness shone brightly and steadily the pale white stars.” Above the horizon hung a sun grown monstrous — a huge, dull-red disc, motionless, that gave no warmth; for the earth had ceased to turn, and one face stared forever into the dying fire of its star.

The crabs, when he looks closer, are fighting — great armoured monsters locked together at the water's edge, tearing at each other with clumsy, irresistible strength, while smaller ones scuttle aside to wait their turn at the remains. It is the struggle for existence, he realises, still going on after thirty million years — stripped now of everything but hunger, the bare engine of life running on in the ruins of the world. He has seen the whole story of mankind between the Eloi and these crabs: the long ascent from the slime, the brief blaze of mind, and the long descent back to the slime again.

There is no wind, no bird, no insect — a stillness like the stillness of a held breath. The sun does not move; it hangs forever at the same height, too dull to cast a proper shadow, too vast to look at steadily. By his watch — absurd, faithful little instrument — he has been gone from his own time only a few hours; by the dials of the machine, thirty million years. He tries to feel the grandeur of it, the awful poetry of standing at the deathbed of the world, and feels only cold, and a loneliness so complete it is like a physical weight.

The sea that lapped the beach was dark red, and bitter cold; the air was thin as mountain air. Nothing green grew; nothing warm lived. And then he saw them, crawling at the water’s edge: “It was a round thing, the size of a football perhaps, or, it may be, bigger, and tentacles trailed down from it; it seemed black against the weltering blood-red water, and it was hopping fitfully about.” Giant crabs — monstrous, mindless — the last heirs of all the teeming life of earth, scuttling and snapping at one another under the huge red sun. He watched them for a while, and a horror of great desolation came upon him.

He travelled on — further still — and stopped again in utter cold and darkness, upon a beach beneath a black sky, where a dark mass blotted out half the stars and something white and butterfly-like flapped feebly in the gloom: the very last flutter of living things. He could bear no more. Loneliness and cold beyond all imagining seized him; he reversed the levers and fled backward through the ages — past the crabs, past the Morlocks, past all the ruin of mankind — until the dials stood once more at his own date, and he stepped down, shaking, into the familiar clutter of his own laboratory, on the very morning he had left it.

It is the last stop that breaks him. The beach is black with cold; the sea is a sheet of ice; overhead, half the sky is blotted out by a vast dark mass — some dead bulk of matter swinging between earth and sun — and in the gloom a pale, butterfly-like thing flaps feebly and falls. This is the end of ends: not a bang, not even a whimper, but a long, slow freezing into dark. He stumbles back to the machine with his teeth chattering, drags the levers over, and flees — backward, homeward — through all the empty millions of years, not daring to stop until the dials read his own sweet, smoky, living century.

The journey home is the loneliest passage in the novel. He does not stop — he dares not stop — but rushes backward through the empty ages with the levers hard over, watching the red sun dwindle and whiten, watching the stars wheel back to their familiar places, with no company but the roaring wind of time and the memory of a little hand slipping from his in the smoke. When at last the dials creep back toward his own date, he is weeping — though whether for Weena, or for mankind, or for himself, he cannot say.

chapters.title: Return — and the Two Flowers
paragraphs: So ends the Time Traveller’s tale, told across the dinner table to his circle of friends. They receive it as such tales are received: the Editor is politely incredulous; the Medical Man shakes his head and reaches for the cigars; Filby argues about the physics of it; the Psychologist sits very still, thinking. Proof? There can be none — except, perhaps, one small thing. From his pocket the Time Traveller draws two strange white flowers, withered now — flowers of a kind unknown to any botanist, flowers that do not grow in England. Weena’s flowers: she had put them into his pockets in the Palace of Green Porcelain, to cheer him among the ruins. He lays them on the little table by the fire, and says nothing more.

The narrator, for his part, hardly knows what to believe — and Wells means us to share his doubt. The story is too wild, too complete, too convenient in its horrors; and yet the man who tells it is unmistakably shattered, and the flowers are unmistakably real. The narrator turns the tale over all that evening, trying it first one way and then another, like a coin of doubtful mintage. By midnight he has decided it must be a dream, a delirium, a magnificent lie — and by morning he believes every word of it again. It is the condition, he implies, in which the reader, too, will be left: balanced forever between doubt and wonder.

The guests crowd round to look. The Medical Man examines the blossoms with professional interest and admits he cannot name them; the Editor turns them over, sniffing at them, half-convinced and half-ashamed of being convinced; Filby declares that a clever man might have had them made — in glass, in wax — though his voice lacks its usual certainty. Only the Psychologist says nothing at all, but sits staring into the fire, turning something over and over in his mind.

The next morning he is gone again. A messenger finds the narrator with a scribbled note: the Time Traveller has taken the machine once more — this time prepared, with a camera and a knapsack, promising to return within the half-hour, bringing photographs and specimens that will convince the most sceptical. The narrator hurries to the laboratory — and waits. The half-hour passes. The machine does not return. Days pass, then months. Three years have gone by as the narrator writes, and the Time Traveller has never come back. He may be lost in time — stranded in some distant age, or fallen, as he feared, into solid rock between one moment and the next.

The Traveller left the flowers in the narrator's keeping that last morning, and the narrator has kept them ever since, though they are brown and brittle now, and crumble at a touch. Sometimes, in the quiet of the evening, he takes them out and looks at them, and thinks of a little white-clad figure putting garlands round a traveller's neck, eight hundred thousand years away. It is a strange comfort. It is the only comfort he has.

And so the novel closes, not with adventure, but with reflection. “He, I know — for the question had been discussed among us long before the Time Machine was made — thought but cheerlessly of the Advancement of Mankind, and saw in the growing pile of civilisation only a foolish heaping that must inevitably fall back upon and destroy its makers in the end.” Was the Traveller right? The narrator cannot say. “But to me the future is still black and blank — is a vast ignorance, lit at a few casual places by the memory of his story. And I have by me, for my comfort, two strange white flowers — shrivelled now, and brown and flat and brittle — to witness that even when mind and strength had gone, gratitude and a mutual tenderness still lived on in the heart of man.”

Three years. The narrator walks past the house in Richmond sometimes, and sees the laboratory windows dark, the garden overgrown, the whole place sinking into the quiet of abandonment — and he thinks of his friend, out there somewhere in the abyss of time, perhaps stranded on some distant shore, perhaps still travelling, perhaps (as he sometimes fears in the small hours) fallen between one moment and the next into that solid rock he always dreaded. He keeps the flowers. He waits. And the future — the future stays black and blank, lit only, here and there, by the memory of a story told one Thursday night over the cigars.
